levels.title: Heart
levels.about: Property parcels in a small city, one row per parcel.

tutorial.text: Click any hex in the painting. Each hex represents a feature, here a property parcel. Its row lights up in the attribute table under the painting, which lists every feature and its fields. Drag the bar above the table to make it bigger or smaller.
Click values next to the land_use field to list every value stored in it. Click a value to drop it into the query box. (Number fields show their range instead.)

Read the first request in the color key, Cream. Build land_use = 'residential' by clicking the field name, the = button and the value, or type it. Click Run. The parcels that match turn cyan: that’s your selection.
In step 2, choose Cream from the gem color menu and click Fill. When every gem for that request is in place, a ✓ appears next to it in the color key.
Now finish Ruby and Blush on your own. Check each field’s type first: floors is a NUMBER, so no quotes. zip looks like a number but is TEXT, so it needs quotes.

lesson: Every hex in the painting is a feature, and every feature has attributes: values stored in fields. Together they make the layer’s attribute table.
A query is a yes/no question asked of every feature. The ones that answer yes get selected.
To ask “is this field equal to this value?” write field = value. Numbers are written plain: acres = 12. Text goes inside single quotes: county = 'Kent'.

Look at each field’s type. Codes that look like numbers, like ZIP codes or phone numbers, are stored as TEXT because you never do math with them. A number field would also drop the leading zero in '02134'.

questions.question: Which query finds parcels where county (a TEXT field) is Kent?
questions.explain: Text values go in single quotes. The field name doesn’t.
hints: Without quotes, SQL thinks Kent is the name of a field.
Double quotes are for field names, not text values.
Quoting the field name turns it into the text 'county', which never equals 'Kent'.

questions.question: A phone field holds values like 6175550142. What type should it be?
questions.explain: You never do math with phone numbers, and a number field would drop leading zeros. It’s a code, so it’s text.
hints: Would you ever add or average phone numbers? And what happens to a leading zero?

levels.title: Sunset
levels.about: Small watersheds across a mountain range, one polygon per watershed.
lesson: Not every question is “equals.” Numbers can be compared: > greater than, < less than, >= greater than or equal to, <= less than or equal to, and <> not equal to.
Watch the edges! pop > 5000 leaves out a town of exactly 5000. pop >= 5000 includes it. Requests say this in words: “more than,” “at least,” “or higher,” “or less.”
Leave commas out of numbers: write 1900, not 1,900.
This table has more fields than you need. Part of the job is figuring out which field answers each request.
Filling a hex replaces any color already there, like pressing a new gem on top. Work down the color key in order. Some colors are used for more than one request.

questions.question: A request asks for watersheds with a mean elevation of at least 850 m. Which condition matches?
questions.explain: “At least” includes 850 itself, so use >=.
hints: > leaves out a watershed at exactly 850 m.
<= picks 850 and everything below it.
= only picks watersheds at exactly 850 m.

questions.question: Which condition is written correctly?
questions.explain: The > comes before the =, and the number has no comma or quotes.
hints: SQL writes it >=, with the > first.
Leave the comma out of numbers.
pop is a number, so its values don’t get quotes.

questions.question: Which watersheds does mean_elev_m <> 400 select?
options: Every watershed except those at exactly 400 m
questions.explain: <> means “not equal to,” so it keeps everything above and below 400 m.
hints: That would be = 400.
<> isn’t “less than”: it means “not equal to.” What about watersheds above 400 m?
<> isn’t “greater than”: it means “not equal to.” What about watersheds below 400 m?

levels.title: Toadstools
levels.about: Field survey plots from a vegetation study, one polygon per plot.
lesson: Sometimes one condition isn’t enough. AND joins two conditions, and a feature is selected only if both are true.
land_use = 'farm' AND acres > 10 selects farms bigger than 10 acres. A small farm fails, and so does a big parking lot.
Each condition needs its own field name: write acres > 10 AND acres < 20, not acres > 10 AND < 20.
Requests rarely say “AND.” Listen for two facts about the same feature: “forest plots where invasive species were found.”

questions.question: Which plots does habitat = 'forest' AND invasive = 'Y' select?
options: Every forest plot, plus every plot with invasive species
Only forest plots that have invasive species
Nothing, because a plot can’t have two values
questions.explain: AND needs both conditions to be true for the same plot.
hints: That’s what OR would do. AND is stricter.
invasive = 'Y' means invasive species were found.
Each condition checks a different field, so one plot can pass both.

questions.question: Which condition finds plots with between 20 and 40 percent canopy (both included)?
questions.explain: Each side of AND is a complete condition with its own field name.
hints: The second condition is missing its field name.
With OR, every plot passes: every number is either at least 20 or at most 40.
No plot can equal 20 and 40 at the same time.

levels.title: Rainbow
levels.about: Zoning districts from a city’s zoning map, one polygon per district.
lesson: OR joins two conditions, and a feature is selected if either one (or both) is true. OR usually selects more features; AND selects fewer.
county = 'Kent' OR county = 'Sussex' selects features in either county.

The classic mistake is county = 'Kent' OR 'Sussex'. It reads fine in English, but SQL sees 'Sussex' as a condition on its own, and it doesn’t mean what you want. Each side of OR needs the field name, the operator and the value.
OR works across different fields too: zone_code = 'INST' OR max_height_ft > 120.

questions.question: Which query selects districts zoned R-1 or R-2?
questions.explain: Each side of OR is a complete condition.
hints: This is the classic trap: the right side is missing zone_code =.
A district can’t have two zone codes at once, so AND selects nothing.
That looks for one district whose code is literally the text “R-1, R-2”.

questions.question: Compared with a AND b, does a OR b select more features or fewer?
questions.explain: OR only needs one condition to be true, so it can only add features.
hints: AND is the strict one: it needs both conditions to be true.

levels.title: Butterfly
levels.about: Census tracts with a few American Community Survey estimates, one polygon per tract.
lesson: When a query mixes AND and OR, SQL does the AND first, the way math does multiplication before addition.
So county = 'Cedar' OR county = 'Dale' AND med_income > 75000 really means county = 'Cedar' OR (county = 'Dale' AND med_income > 75000): every Cedar tract, plus the wealthier Dale tracts.
Parentheses say what goes together: (county = 'Cedar' OR county = 'Dale') AND med_income > 75000 means wealthier tracts in either county.
When a query has both AND and OR, use parentheses every time, even when you think you don’t need them.

questions.question: SQL does AND before OR. Which query means the same as a OR b AND c?
questions.explain: AND binds tighter, so b AND c is grouped first.
hints: That’s what you usually want, which is why you need to write the parentheses.

questions.question: Which query selects tracts in Cedar or Dale County with more than 50% renters?
questions.explain: The parentheses keep the two counties together, and the renter test applies to both.
hints: Without parentheses, every Cedar tract is selected, renters or not.
This is how SQL reads the first option: all of Cedar, plus Dale tracts with many renters.
A tract can’t be in two counties at once.

levels.title: Cactus
levels.about: Public-land grazing allotments across several western states, one polygon per allotment.
lesson: IN is a shortcut for a list of ORs: state IN ('AZ', 'NM', 'NV') means the same as state = 'AZ' OR state = 'NM' OR state = 'NV'.
NOT flips a condition: NOT status = 'Active' selects everything that isn’t Active. You can also write status <> 'Active'. NOT IN works too: state NOT IN ('AZ', 'NM').
BETWEEN is a shortcut for a range: yr BETWEEN 2015 AND 2018 means yr >= 2015 AND yr <= 2018. Both ends are included.

questions.question: Does last_eval_yr BETWEEN 2015 AND 2018 select an allotment evaluated in 2018?
questions.explain: BETWEEN includes both ends of the range.
hints: BETWEEN is inclusive: it means >= 2015 AND <= 2018.

questions.question: Which query means the same as state IN ('AZ', 'NM')?
questions.explain: IN is a list of ORs.
hints: An allotment can only be in one state, so AND selects nothing.
That looks for the literal text “AZ, NM”.
BETWEEN on text compares alphabetically, so it would also catch states like CO and ID.

levels.title: Fish
levels.about: Named lakes, ponds, reservoirs and swamps, modeled on the National Hydrography Dataset. One polygon per waterbody.
lesson: = only matches text exactly. LIKE matches a pattern, using wildcards.
% stands for any number of characters (even none). gnis_name LIKE '%Pond' finds names that end in “Pond.” LIKE 'Mill%' finds names that start with “Mill.” LIKE '%Spring%' finds “Spring” anywhere.
_ (underscore) stands for exactly one character: LIKE '_ake' matches “Lake” and “Make” but not “Snake.”
Heads up: in this tool (SQLite), LIKE ignores capital letters, so '%pond' also matches “Pond.” Many databases are case-sensitive, so match the capitals you see in the data.

questions.question: Which names does gnis_name LIKE 'Mill%' match?
questions.explain: 'Mill%' means the name starts with “Mill,” followed by anything.
hints: “Sawmill Pond” doesn’t start with Mill.
The % allows more characters after “Mill.”
That would be '%Mill%', with a wildcard on both sides.

questions.question: What does _ stand for in a LIKE pattern?
questions.explain: _ is a single-character wildcard; % matches any number.
hints: That’s %.
It matches any one character, including a space.
Inside LIKE it’s a wildcard.

levels.title: Night skyline
levels.about: Building and lot footprints from a downtown survey, one polygon per footprint. Some values were never recorded.
lesson: Real data has gaps. When a value was never recorded, the field holds NULL: not zero, not blank text, just “no value.” The attribute table shows it as <Null>.
To find missing values, write field IS NULL. To find values that are there, write field IS NOT NULL.
The trap: field = NULL never selects anything, because nothing is “equal” to an unknown, not even another unknown.
NULLs also drop out of comparisons: height_ft < 50 skips every footprint whose height is NULL.

questions.question: What does height_ft = NULL select?
options: Every footprint with a height of 0
questions.explain: Nothing is ever equal to NULL. Use IS NULL instead.
hints: That’s what you want, but you have to write height_ft IS NULL.
NULL isn’t 0. Zero is a value; NULL means there’s no value.
It selects nothing, because the comparison is never true.

questions.question: Does height_ft < 50 select footprints whose height is NULL?
questions.explain: A missing height isn’t less than 50, or more than 50. It’s unknown, so it’s skipped.
hints: An unknown value can’t be compared, so those footprints are left out.

levels.title: Flower
levels.about: Crop fields reported by farms in one county, one polygon per field.
lesson: So far every query made a new selection. The selection type menu lets a query change the selection you already have instead:

Add to the current selection keeps what’s selected and adds the new matches. Remove from the current selection takes the new matches away. Select subset from the current selection keeps only the selected features that also match.

This is how GIS users build a complicated selection step by step, checking the count after each step. Some of these requests could be written as one query with AND, OR and NOT. Try building them in steps instead.

questions.question: All corn fields are selected. You run irrigated = 'Y' with Remove from the current selection. What’s left?
questions.explain: Remove takes the irrigated fields out of the selection, leaving the rest of the corn.
hints: That’s what select subset would give you.
Remove only works on what’s already selected, and only corn was selected.
Only the irrigated corn is removed.

questions.question: Soybean fields are selected. Which selection type lets you also select the large hay fields?
options: Select subset from the current selection
questions.explain: Add keeps the soybeans and puts the hay fields on top.
hints: A new selection would drop the soybeans.
Remove would take hay fields away, and none are selected yet.
Subset keeps only fields that are already selected and match, and no soybean field is a hay field.

levels.title: Outlined cat
levels.dataset: Land ownership around Pine Ridge State Forest
levels.about: Land parcels in and around a state forest, one polygon per parcel.
lesson: Attribute queries ask about a feature’s values. Select by Location asks where a feature is in relation to other features.

Here the parcels are compared with the parcels you’ve already selected. Boundary touches picks parcels whose boundaries touch a selected parcel. Intersect picks parcels that share any area or boundary, so it also picks the selected parcels themselves.
Combine tools with the selection type: new replaces the selection, add to adds, remove from takes away, and select subset keeps only the parcels that pass the new test too.
Nothing in the attribute table says which parcels are next to the forest. Some questions can only be answered by location!

questions.question: You select one parcel, then run Intersect against it. Which parcels end up selected?
options: The parcel itself and its neighbors
questions.explain: Intersect includes anything that shares space or a boundary, and a parcel shares space with itself.
hints: That’s Boundary touches. Does a parcel intersect itself?
Its neighbors share a boundary with it, and a shared boundary counts as intersecting.
Only parcels that share space or a boundary with the selected one.

questions.question: You have the forest selected and want only the private parcels that touch it. After running Boundary touches, what’s the next step?
options: Run owner_type = 'private' with select subset from the current selection
Run owner_type = 'private' with add to the current selection
Nothing; Boundary touches already removed the forest
questions.explain: Subset keeps only the touching parcels that are also private.
hints: A new selection throws away the location result and selects every private parcel.
Adding would pile every private parcel onto the selection.
Forest parcels touch other forest parcels too, so they’re still in the selection.

levels.title: Glowing moon
levels.skill: Select by Location: within a distance
levels.about: Parcels in and around a dark-sky preserve with an observatory, one polygon per parcel.
lesson: Within a distance selects features that are no farther than a set distance from the selected features, like asking “what’s within 300 m of here?”
Distance is measured edge to edge, from the nearest boundary of one feature to the nearest boundary of the other. Neighbors that share a boundary are 0 m apart.
The selected features are within 0 m of themselves, so they’re always included. If you only want the features around them, take the originals out afterward with Remove from the current selection.
Always check the units. In this layer, distances are in meters.

questions.question: You select the observatory and run Within a distance of 300 m. Is the observatory itself in the result?
questions.explain: It’s 0 m from itself, which is within 300 m. Remove it afterward if you only want its surroundings.
hints: Distance is measured edge to edge, and a feature is 0 m from itself.

questions.question: How is the distance between two parcels measured here?
questions.explain: GIS measures the shortest distance between the two shapes, which is between their nearest edges.
hints: Center to center would be farther for big parcels.
It’s the shortest gap between the two shapes, wherever that is.
That would be a network analysis, a different tool.

levels.title: Pond and trail
levels.skill: Location vs. other layers: within, contains, crossed by
levels.about: Small parcels around a pond, one polygon per parcel. Three other layers sit on top: the pond, a trail and some springs.
lesson: So far you’ve compared parcels with other parcels. Select by Location can also compare them with a different layer. This level has three: a pond (polygon), a trail (line) and springs (points). They’re drawn on top of the painting.
Intersect selects parcels that share any space with the other layer: a parcel half in the pond intersects it, and so does a parcel the trail passes through.
Are completely within selects parcels that lie entirely inside the other layer’s shape, with no part sticking out.
Completely contain is the reverse: parcels that have a whole feature of the other layer inside them, like a spring.
Choose the other layer in the Selecting features menu.

questions.question: A parcel is half in the pond and half on land. Which is true?
options: It intersects the pond and is completely within it
It intersects the pond but is not completely within it
It is completely within the pond but doesn’t intersect it
questions.explain: It shares space with the pond, so it intersects, but part of it sticks out, so it isn’t completely within.
hints: Part of the parcel is on land, so it isn’t completely within.
Anything completely within the pond also intersects it.
It does share space with the pond.

questions.question: Which relationship finds the parcels that have a spring inside them?
questions.explain: The parcel contains the spring.
hints: A parcel can’t be within a point; it’s the other way around.
A spring point inside a parcel isn’t on its boundary.

levels.title: Hot air balloon
levels.about: Tax parcels from a county assessor, with the short, all-caps field names that assessor data usually has. One polygon per parcel.
lesson: This painting uses everything: comparisons, AND, OR, parentheses, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, NULL, selection types and Select by Location.

Real datasets rarely have friendly field names. Here they’re short and all caps, like LU_CODE and YR_BLT. Read the field descriptions (the metadata) before you write a query, and click values to see how codes are actually stored.
Plan each request before you type: which field, which operator, which values? Does it need more than one step?

questions.question: A field called ASSD_VAL could mean several things. Where should you look to find out?
questions.explain: Metadata tells you what a field holds, its units and how its values are coded.
hints: Guessing leads to wrong answers that look right.
The painting isn’t part of the data.

questions.question: Which query finds AG parcels in ZIP 05301 or 05346?
questions.explain: Parentheses keep the two ZIP codes together, and ZIP is text, so its values need quotes.
hints: Without parentheses, every parcel in 05346 is selected, AG or not.
ZIP is a TEXT field, and each side of OR needs a complete condition.
